title: Ὁ Ὀδυσσεὺς σῴζεται
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Socus’ spear goes through Odysseus’ shield and breastplate, but Athena keeps it from his flesh. Odysseus tells Socus he is doomed, stabs him in the back as he turns to run, and vaunts over him, saying that birds will have the body, while the Achaeans will bury Odysseus if he dies. Wounded, he draws the spear out and shouts for help; Menelaus hears and fetches Ajax. They find Odysseus ringed by Trojans like jackals round a wounded deer, until Ajax comes up like a lion, the Trojans scatter, and Menelaus leads Odysseus out. Ajax then kills and wounds Trojans, rushing across the plain like a flooded river. Hector, fighting far off on the left, has not yet heard of it. There Alexander shoots the healer Machaon in the shoulder. Idomeneus tells Nestor to carry Machaon off to the ships, and Nestor does. Cebriones points out Ajax to Hector, and Hector drives into the Achaean ranks, taking care to avoid Ajax.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν οὔτησε κατ’ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn outēse kat’ aspida pantos’ eïsēn.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he thrust at him, upon the shield equal on every side.
sentences.i: With these words he stabbed at him on his shield, which was equal on every side.
sentences.n: Socus, whose speech closed the last part, now throws; ὣς εἰπὼν ‘so having spoken’ ties the thrust to his words, and the man he strikes at, Odysseus, is not named. οὔτησε is the aorist of οὐτάω, a thrust from close at hand, which usually means ‘wounded’; here the point lands on the shield and wounds no one yet (the next unit tells how far it went), so the English says ‘thrust at’. κατ’ ἀσπίδα is ‘upon the shield’, and πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην ‘equal on every side’ is the stock phrase for a well-balanced shield (ἐΐση is the longer form of ἴση).

sentences.t:
διὰ μὲν ἀσπίδος ἦλθε φαεινῆς ὄβριμον ἔγχος,
καὶ διὰ θώρηκος πολυδαιδάλου ἠρήρειστο,
πάντα δ’ ἀπὸ πλευρῶν χρόα ἔργαθεν, οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἔασε
Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη μιχθήμεναι ἔγκασι φωτός.
sentences.tr:
dia men aspidos ēlthe phaeinēs obrimon enchos,
kai dia thōrēkos polydaidalou ērēreisto,
panta d’ apo pleurōn chroa ergathen, oud’ et’ ease
Pallas Athēnaiē michthēmenai enkasi phōtos.
sentences.l:
Through the shining shield went the mighty spear,
and through the much-wrought breastplate it was driven,
and from the ribs all the flesh it kept off, and no longer allowed
Pallas Athena that it should mingle with the entrails of the man.
sentences.i: The mighty spear went through the shining shield, and was driven through the richly wrought breastplate as well; it kept off all the flesh from the ribs, and Pallas Athena would not let it go on to mingle with the entrails of the man.
sentences.n: The spear goes through two layers of defence and is then stopped by the goddess. Lines 435–436 are 3.357–358 word for word. Line 435 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of διά is scanned long (δῑά) to fill the long place of the first foot. ἔργαθεν is an aorist of ἔργω ‘shut out, keep off’ (ἀπό can be taken with it or with πλευρῶν, and the English takes ‘from the ribs’), and the Greek does not name its subject: the spear that kept clear of the flesh and the breastplate that kept the flesh away from the spear both fit, so the English keeps a bare ‘it’. οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἔασε is ‘no longer allowed’, ἔασε taking an infinitive; μιχθήμεναι is the aorist passive infinitive of μίγνυμι in the epic ending -μεναι (Attic μιχθῆναι), ‘to be mingled’. ἔγκασι is a dative plural of ἔγκατα ‘entrails’, and φωτός ‘of the man’ is the Homeric word φώς, φωτός. Athena’s help for Odysseus is stated, not shown: the poet gives no other cause.

sentences.t:
γνῶ δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ὅ οἱ οὔ τι τέλος κατακαίριον ἦλθεν,
ἂψ δ’ ἀναχωρήσας Σῶκον πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr:
gnō d’ Odyseus ho hoi ou ti telos katakairion ēlthen,
aps d’ anachōrēsas Sōkon pros mython eeipen·
sentences.l:
And Odysseus knew that to him no deadly end had come,
and back, stepping back, he addressed Socus with a word:
sentences.i: Odysseus knew that no deadly end had come to him, and, stepping back, he spoke to Socus:
sentences.n: γνῶ is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise, realise’ without its augment (Attic ἔγνω); ὅ is ‘that’ (= ὅτι) and οἱ ‘to him’. τέλος is the end or outcome of the blow, and κατακαίριον ‘deadly’ is a rare word built on καίριος ‘in the vital place’, so its sense is taken from the context. ἂψ ‘back’ goes with ἀναχωρήσας ‘stepping back’; ἔειπεν is the epic form of εἶπεν, and πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν ‘addressed with a word’ is the formula that introduces many speeches.

sentences.t: ἆ δείλ’ ἦ μάλα δή σε κιχάνεται αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος.
sentences.tr: a deil’ ē mala dē se kichanetai aipys olethros.
sentences.l: “Oh, miserable one, truly now does steep destruction reach you.
sentences.i: “Oh, miserable man, steep destruction is truly reaching you.
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks to Socus. ἆ δείλ’ is the cry of address ‘oh, miserable one’: δείλ’ is δειλέ, the vocative of δειλός, with its final vowel elided. ἦ μάλα δή strengthens the statement (‘truly now’), and κιχάνεται, from κιχάνω ‘reach, overtake’, has σε ‘you’ as its object. αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος ‘steep destruction’ is a formula; ‘steep’ makes the ruin something with no foothold to escape by.

sentences.t: ἤτοι μέν ῥ’ ἔμ’ ἔπαυσας ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr: ētoi men rh’ em’ epausas epi Trōessi machesthai·
sentences.l: Indeed, on the one hand, you have made me stop fighting against the Trojans;
sentences.i: Indeed you have made me stop fighting against the Trojans;
sentences.n: ἤτοι (one word in this edition) with μέν looks ahead to δέ in the next line: ‘indeed … but’. ἔπαυσας is the aorist of παύω ‘make stop’ with the accusative ἔμ’ ‘me’ and the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’; ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι (dative plural in -εσσι) is ‘against the Trojans’. Odysseus means that Socus has put an end to his fighting for the moment.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ ἐγὼ ἐνθάδε φημὶ φόνον καὶ κῆρα μέλαιναν
ἤματι τῷδ’ ἔσσεσθαι, ἐμῷ δ’ ὑπὸ δουρὶ δαμέντα
εὖχος ἐμοὶ δώσειν, ψυχὴν δ’ Ἄϊδι κλυτοπώλῳ.
sentences.tr:
soi d’ egō enthade phēmi phonon kai kēra melainan
ēmati tōid’ essesthai, emōi d’ hypo douri damenta
euchos emoi dōsein, psychēn d’ Aïdi klytopōlōi.
sentences.l:
And to you I say here slaughter and the black death-fate
on this day to be, and, subdued under my spear,
a boast to me you will give, and your soul to Hades of the famous horses.”
sentences.i: But I say that here, on this day, slaughter and the black spirit of death will be yours, and that, overcome under my spear, you will give me the triumph and your soul to Hades of the famous horses.”
sentences.n: The threat is built on φημί ‘I say’ with infinitives: ἔσσεσθαι (future infinitive of εἰμί, ‘to be’) has φόνον and κῆρα μέλαιναν as its subjects, and δώσειν (future infinitive of δίδωμι) has σε ‘you’ understood, which δαμέντα ‘subdued’ (aorist passive participle of δαμάζω) agrees with. κήρ is the ‘death-fate’ that carries a man off, not the neuter κῆρ ‘heart’. εὖχος is what a victor wins by killing, a boast or triumph. Lines 443 and 445 are 5.652 and 5.654 word for word. Ἄϊδι is the dative of Ἄϊς, a by-form of Ἅιδης, and κλυτοπώλῳ ‘of the famous horses’ is κλυτός ‘famous’ + πῶλος ‘foal, horse’; why Hades has this epithet is not known. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ, καὶ ὃ μὲν φύγαδ’ αὖτις ὑποστρέψας ἐβεβήκει,
τῷ δὲ μεταστρεφθέντι μεταφρένῳ ἐν δόρυ πῆξεν
ὤμων μεσσηγύς, διὰ δὲ στήθεσφιν ἔλασσε,
δούπησεν δὲ πεσών·
sentences.tr:
ē, kai ho men phygad’ autis hypostrepsas ebebēkei,
tōi de metastrephthenti metaphrenōi en dory pēxen
ōmōn messēgys, dia de stēthesphin elasse,
doupēsen de pesōn·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and the one, for his part, to flight again, turning back, had set off,
and to him, as he turned about, in the back the spear he fixed,
between the shoulders, and through the chest he drove it,
and he fell with a thud;
sentences.i: He spoke, and the other had turned back and started off in flight again; but as he turned about, Odysseus fixed his spear in his back, between the shoulders, and drove it through his chest, and he fell with a thud;
sentences.n: ἦ, καί ‘he spoke, and’ closes a speech and turns the story; ἦ is a past tense of ἠμί ‘say’. ὁ μέν is the pronoun ‘that one’, Socus, and the contrast with Odysseus is carried by the pronouns, not by names. φύγαδ’ is ‘to flight’ with the suffix -δε of direction, and ἐβεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had set off’. τῷ … μεταστρεφθέντι is a dative, ‘to him as he turned about’, and μεταφρένῳ ‘in the back’; Odysseus is the subject of πῆξεν ‘fixed’, understood. Lines 447–449, as far as πεσών, are the stock description of a spear in the back (see 8.258–259 and 5.40–42). δούπησεν δὲ πεσών is ‘and he fell with a thud’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 449.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἐπεύξατο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ho d’ epeuxato dios Odysseus·
sentences.l: and he vaunted, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: and heavenly Odysseus cried out in triumph over him:
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 449. ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’, the change of subject back to Odysseus. ἐπεύξατο is the aorist of ἐπεύχομαι, which means ‘pray’ in a prayer but ‘vaunt, cry out in triumph’ over a fallen enemy, as here. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ὦ Σῶχ’ Ἱππάσου υἱὲ δαΐφρονος ἱπποδάμοιο
φθῆ σε τέλος θανάτοιο κιχήμενον, οὐδ’ ὑπάλυξας.
sentences.tr:
ō Sōch’ Hippasou huie daïphronos hippodamoio
phthē se telos thanatoio kichēmenon, oud’ hypalyxas.
sentences.l:
“O Socus, son of Hippasus, wise-minded, horse-taming,
the end of death was first to reach you, and you did not escape.
sentences.i: “Socus, son of Hippasus, wise-hearted tamer of horses, the end of death was first to reach you, and you did not escape it.
sentences.n: Odysseus now speaks over the dead man. Σῶχ’ is the vocative Σῶκε, elided, with κ turned to χ before the rough breathing of Ἱππάσου. Ἱππάσου, δαΐφρονος and ἱπποδάμοιο are genitives agreeing with each other, ‘of Hippasus, wise-minded, horse-taming’, the last in -οιο (= -ου); whether δαΐφρων means ‘wise’ (from δαῆναι) or ‘fierce’ (from δαΐ, ‘in war’) is disputed. φθῆ is the aorist of φθάνω ‘be first’ without augment, and it takes a participle: κιχήμενον (neuter, agreeing with τέλος) ‘reaching’, with σε its object. τέλος θανάτοιο is ‘the end of death’. ὑπάλυξας is the aorist of ὑπαλύσκω ‘escape from under’.

sentences.t:
ἆ δείλ’ οὐ μὲν σοί γε πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
ὄσσε καθαιρήσουσι θανόντι περ, ἀλλ’ οἰωνοὶ
ὠμησταὶ ἐρύουσι, περὶ πτερὰ πυκνὰ βαλόντες.
sentences.tr:
a deil’ ou men soi ge patēr kai potnia mētēr
osse kathairēsousi thanonti per, all’ oiōnoi
ōmēstai eryousi, peri ptera pykna balontes.
sentences.l:
Oh, miserable one, not indeed for you will father and lady mother
close the eyes, dead though you are, but birds,
raw-feeding, will drag at you, thick wings around you having cast.
sentences.i: Oh, miserable man, your father and your lady mother will not close your eyes, dead though you are; instead, birds that feed on raw flesh will drag at you, flinging their thick wings about you.
sentences.n: Burial was owed to the dead, and the family’s first duty was to close the eyes; Odysseus tells Socus he will be denied it. οὐ μέν … γε is ‘not indeed’, σοί the dative ‘for you’, and ὄσσε the dual ‘the two eyes’. θανόντι περ is a dative participle with concessive περ, ‘dead though you are’. πότνια μήτηρ is the formula ‘lady mother’. ὠμησταί ‘eaters of raw flesh’ (ὠμός ‘raw’) is a rare word, here an adjective of the birds. ἐρύουσι looks like a present but the sense is future, as with καθαιρήσουσι; ἐρύω is ‘drag, draw’. περὶ … βαλόντες is tmesis: ‘having cast thick wings around’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἔμ’, εἴ κε θάνω, κτεριοῦσί γε δῖοι Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr: autar em’, ei ke thanō, kteriousi ge dioi Achaioi.
sentences.l: But me, if I die, will render funeral rites to, indeed, the heavenly Achaeans.”
sentences.i: But as for me, if I should die, the heavenly Achaeans will pay me funeral honours.”
sentences.n: The contrast with Socus: αὐτὰρ ἔμ’ … κτεριοῦσί γε ‘but me … they will indeed’. εἴ κε θάνω is the aorist subjunctive, ‘if I should die’. κτεριοῦσι is the future of κτερίζω ‘give funeral rites’ (from κτέρεα, the offerings given to the dead). δῖοι Ἀχαιοί ‘the heavenly Achaeans’ is the stock phrase, with δῖος translated the same way as everywhere. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν Σώκοιο δαΐφρονος ὄβριμον ἔγχος
ἔξω τε χροὸς ἕλκε καὶ ἀσπίδος ὀμφαλοέσσης·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn Sōkoio daïphronos obrimon enchos
exō te chroos helke kai aspidos omphaloessēs·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, of Socus, wise-minded, the mighty spear
out from the flesh he drew, and from the bossed shield;
sentences.i: With these words he drew the mighty spear of wise-hearted Socus out of his flesh and out of his bossed shield;
sentences.n: The spear that Socus threw is still in Odysseus: it has lodged in his shield and grazed his flesh, and he now pulls it out. Σώκοιο is the genitive in -οιο (= -ου), δαΐφρονος again ‘wise-minded’ (sense disputed), and ἕλκε an imperfect without augment. ἔξω … χροὸς καὶ ἀσπίδος is ‘out from the flesh and from the shield’, genitives of separation. ὀμφαλοέσσης is ‘bossed’: ὀμφαλός means ‘navel’ and also the boss at the centre of a shield.

sentences.t: αἷμα δέ οἱ σπασθέντος ἀνέσσυτο, κῆδε δὲ θυμόν.
sentences.tr: haima de hoi spasthentos anessyto, kēde de thymon.
sentences.l: and for him, as it was drawn out, the blood rushed up, and it distressed his spirit.
sentences.i: When the spear was drawn out, blood rushed up from him, and it distressed his spirit.
sentences.n: σπασθέντος is an aorist passive participle of σπάω ‘draw’, genitive absolute with the spear understood: ‘it having been drawn out’. οἱ is ‘for him, from him’. ἀνέσσυτο is the aorist of σεύομαι ‘rush’ with ἀνά ‘up’. κῆδε is the imperfect of transitive κήδω ‘distress’, with θυμόν ‘spirit’ as the part affected; the subject, left unspoken, is the blood or the wound.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δὲ μεγάθυμοι ὅπως ἴδον αἷμ’ Ὀδυσῆος
κεκλόμενοι καθ’ ὅμιλον ἐπ’ αὐτῷ πάντες ἔβησαν.
sentences.tr:
Trōes de megathymoi hopōs idon haim’ Odysēos
keklomenoi kath’ homilon ep’ autōi pantes ebēsan.
sentences.l:
And the Trojans, great-hearted, when they saw the blood of Odysseus,
calling out, through the throng upon him all went.
sentences.i: And when the great-hearted Trojans saw the blood of Odysseus, they called out and all went at him through the throng.
sentences.n: The Trojans see blood and attack. μεγάθυμοι ‘great-hearted’ is the stock epithet and is used of Trojans and Achaeans alike. ὅπως is ‘when’ (= ὡς), and ἴδον is the aorist of εἶδον without augment. κεκλόμενοι is a reduplicated aorist participle of κέλομαι, usually ‘urge’; here ‘calling out’. ἔβησαν is the aorist of βαίνω, and ἐπ’ αὐτῷ … ἔβησαν is ‘went at him’. Ὀδυσῆος is the form with one σ, the same man as Ὀδυσσῆος in 466.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἐξοπίσω ἀνεχάζετο, αὖε δ’ ἑταίρους.
sentences.tr: autar ho g’ exopisō anechazeto, aue d’ hetairous.
sentences.l: But he to the rear was drawing back, and called to his companions.
sentences.i: But he kept drawing back toward the rear, and called out to his companions.
sentences.n: ὅ γ’ is ‘he, for his part’. ἀνεχάζετο is the imperfect of ἀναχάζομαι ‘draw back’, and ἐξοπίσω ‘to the rear’; αὖε is the imperfect of αὔω ‘call out’. Odysseus gives ground step by step and shouts for help, as the next two lines show.

sentences.t:
τρὶς μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἤϋσεν ὅσον κεφαλὴ χάδε φωτός,
τρὶς δ’ ἄϊεν ἰάχοντος ἄρηι φίλος Μενέλαος.
sentences.tr:
tris men epeit’ ēÿsen hoson kephalē chade phōtos,
tris d’ aïen iachontos arēi philos Menelaos.
sentences.l:
Three times then he shouted as much as a man’s head held,
and three times heard him, as he cried out, Menelaus, dear to Ares.
sentences.i: Three times, then, he shouted as loud as a man’s head can hold, and three times Menelaus, dear to Ares, heard him cry out.
sentences.n: τρὶς μέν … τρὶς δέ sets the two threefold actions side by side. ἤϋσεν is the aorist of ἀΰω ‘shout’. ὅσον κεφαλὴ χάδε φωτός is ‘as much as a man’s head held’, the loudest a man can shout; χάδε is an aorist of χανδάνω ‘hold, contain’ without augment. ἄϊεν is the imperfect of ἀΐω ‘hear’ without augment, taking the genitive ἰάχοντος (participle) ‘as he cried out’. ἄρηι φίλος is ‘dear to Ares’.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἄρ’ Αἴαντα προσεφώνεεν ἐγγὺς ἐόντα·
sentences.tr: aipsa d’ ar’ Aianta prosephōneen engys eonta·
sentences.l: And at once then to Ajax he spoke, who was near:
sentences.i: And at once he spoke to Ajax, who was near him:
sentences.n: The speaker is Menelaus, who has just heard the shout. The line is a formula, as at 9.201 (αἶψα δὲ Πάτροκλον …) and the Odyssey’s 22.163, with another name. προσεφώνεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘address’, and ἐγγὺς ἐόντα ‘being near’ qualifies Ajax. αἶψα is ‘at once’ here.

sentences.t:
Αἶαν διογενὲς Τελαμώνιε κοίρανε λαῶν
ἀμφί μ’ Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος ἵκετ’ ἀϋτὴ
τῷ ἰκέλη ὡς εἴ ἑ βιῴατο μοῦνον ἐόντα
Τρῶες ἀποτμήξαντες ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ.
sentences.tr:
Aian diogenes Telamōnie koirane laōn
amphi m’ Odyssēos talasiphronos hiket’ aÿtē
tōi ikelē hōs ei he biōiato mounon eonta
Trōes apotmēxantes eni kraterēi hysminēi.
sentences.l:
“Ajax, Zeus-sprung, Telamonian, ruler of the people,
around me of Odysseus, enduring-minded, has come the battle-cry,
like that, as if they were overpowering him, being alone,
the Trojans, having cut him off in the strong battle.
sentences.i: “Zeus-born Ajax, Telamonian, ruler of the people, the battle-cry of steadfast Odysseus has come to me, and it is as if the Trojans were overpowering him, cut off and alone in the strong battle.
sentences.n: Menelaus speaks to Ajax. The first line is 7.234 word for word: all vocatives, διογενές ‘Zeus-sprung’, Τελαμώνιε ‘Telamonian’, κοίρανε ‘ruler’. ἀμφί … ἵκετ’ is ‘has come around me’ (ἵκετο without augment), and ἀϋτή is the ‘battle-cry’. ταλασίφρων is ‘enduring-minded’ (τλῆναι ‘endure’ + φρήν). τῷ ἰκέλη is ‘like that’, the cry like what would be heard ὡς εἴ … βιῴατο ‘as if they were overpowering’; βιῴατο is the optative of βιάομαι ‘use force on’, ἑ is ‘him’ with μοῦνον ἐόντα ‘being alone’, and ἀποτμήξαντες is the aorist participle of ἀποτμήγω ‘cut off’. κρατερὴ ὑσμίνη is ‘strong battle’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν καθ’ ὅμιλον·
sentences.tr: all’ iomen kath’ homilon·
sentences.l: But let us go through the throng;
sentences.i: But let us go through the throng;
sentences.n: ἴομεν is the short-vowel subjunctive of εἶμι ‘go’, an exhortation: ‘let us go’. καθ’ ὅμιλον is ‘through the throng’.

sentences.t: ἀλεξέμεναι γὰρ ἄμεινον.
sentences.tr: alexemenai gar ameinon.
sentences.l: for to defend is better.
sentences.i: for it is better to defend him.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 469. ἀλεξέμεναι is the infinitive of ἀλέξω ‘ward off, defend’, in the epic ending -έμεναι; Odysseus, the object, is left to be understood. ἄμεινον is the comparative ‘better’.

sentences.t:
δείδω μή τι πάθῃσιν ἐνὶ Τρώεσσι μονωθεὶς
ἐσθλὸς ἐών, μεγάλη δὲ ποθὴ Δαναοῖσι γένηται.
sentences.tr:
deidō mē ti pathēisin eni Trōessi monōtheis
esthlos eōn, megalē de pothē Danaoisi genētai.
sentences.l:
I fear lest he suffer something among the Trojans, left alone,
being good, and a great lack for the Danaans come to be.”
sentences.i: I fear that he may suffer something among the Trojans, left alone, good man that he is, and that a great lack of him may come upon the Danaans.”
sentences.n: δείδω μή with the subjunctive is ‘I fear lest’. πάθῃσιν (from πάσχω) with τι ‘something’ is a way of not saying ‘be killed’. μονωθείς is an aorist passive participle, ‘left alone’ (μόνος). ἐσθλὸς ἐών is ‘being good’, and in a battle this means brave. ποθή is a ‘lack’, the felt absence of a man; ‘of him’ is understood, and the house word is the one used at 1.240. γένηται is the aorist subjunctive of γίγνομαι. Here Menelaus gives his reason for hurrying; the speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὃ μὲν ἦρχ’, ὃ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕσπετο ἰσόθεος φώς.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn ho men ērch’, ho d’ ham’ hespeto isotheos phōs.
sentences.l: So having spoken, the one led the way, and the other followed along, a man equal to a god.
sentences.i: So he spoke and led the way, and the other followed with him, a man the equal of a god.
sentences.n: ὃ μέν … ὃ δ’ ‘the one … the other’: Menelaus leads and Ajax follows. ἦρχ’ is the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead the way’ and ἕσπετο the aorist of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, with ἅμ’ ‘along’. ἰσόθεος φώς ‘a man equal to a god’ is a stock phrase, translated every time.

sentences.t: εὗρον ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆα Διῒ φίλον·
sentences.tr: heuron epeit’ Odysēa Diï philon·
sentences.l: They found then Odysseus, dear to Zeus;
sentences.i: Then they found Odysseus, dear to Zeus;
sentences.n: εὗρον is plural, ‘they found’: Menelaus and Ajax, though no subject is named. Διῒ φίλον ‘dear to Zeus’ is the stock phrase (the edition prints the diaeresis on Διῒ). The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 473.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτὸν
Τρῶες ἕπονθ’ ὡς εἴ τε δαφοινοὶ θῶες ὄρεσφιν
ἀμφ’ ἔλαφον κεραὸν βεβλημένον, ὅν τ’ ἔβαλ’ ἀνὴρ
ἰῷ ἀπὸ νευρῆς·
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ar’ auton
Trōes heponth’ hōs ei te daphoinoi thōes oresphin
amph’ elaphon keraon beblēmenon, hon t’ ebal’ anēr
iōi apo neurēs·
sentences.l:
and around him, then,
the Trojans kept close, just as when deep-red jackals in the mountains
around a horned deer that has been hit, which a man hit
with an arrow from the string;
sentences.i: and the Trojans kept close about him, as deep-red jackals do in the mountains around a horned deer that a man has hit with an arrow from the bowstring;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 473. The first of the part’s two similes: the Trojans are jackals round a wounded deer. ἕπονθ’ is the imperfect plural of ἕπω/ἕπομαι (the θ is the aspirate that elision produces before the rough breathing of ὡς); ἕπω with ἀμφί means ‘be busy about’, so ‘kept close’. ὡς εἴ τε is ‘just as when’. δαφοινοί is δα- (intensive) + φοινός ‘red’; whether it means tawny, blood-red or reddened with gore is not known, and ‘deep-red’ is the house word. θῶες are jackals; ὄρεσφιν is ‘in the mountains’ with the suffix -φιν. κεραόν is ‘horned’, βεβλημένον ‘hit’, ἔβαλ’ ‘has hit’ (a plain aorist: the shot comes before the chase, so the English has the perfect). ἰῷ is the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’.

sentences.t:
τὸν μέν τ’ ἤλυξε πόδεσσι
φεύγων, ὄφρ’ αἷμα λιαρὸν καὶ γούνατ’ ὀρώρῃ·
sentences.tr:
ton men t’ ēlyxe podessi
pheugōn, ophr’ haima liaron kai gounat’ orōrēi·
sentences.l:
him, indeed, it escapes with its feet,
fleeing, as long as its blood is warm and its knees can move;
sentences.i: it escapes the man on its feet, fleeing, as long as its blood is warm and its knees can move;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 476. ἤλυξε is the aorist of ἀλύσκω ‘escape’, used of what always happens, so the English has the present; the same goes for the aorists that follow in the simile. The deer is the subject and τὸν ‘him’ the man who shot it. ὄφρα … ὀρώρῃ is the perfect subjunctive of ὄρνυμι ‘stir’, ‘as long as … is stirred’, with αἷμα λιαρόν ‘warm blood’ and γούνατ’ ‘knees’; ‘can move’ is what the stirring of the knees means.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ τόν γε δαμάσσεται ὠκὺς ὀϊστός,
ὠμοφάγοι μιν θῶες ἐν οὔρεσι δαρδάπτουσιν
ἐν νέμεϊ σκιερῷ·
sentences.tr:
autar epei dē ton ge damassetai ōkys oïstos,
ōmophagoi min thōes en ouresi dardaptousin
en nemeï skierōi·
sentences.i: but when the swift arrow subdues it, jackals that eat raw flesh tear it apart in the mountains, in a shady glen;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δή answers μέν in 476: ‘but when’. δαμάσσεται is the subjunctive of δαμάζω ‘subdue’ (as the same verb in 444), τόν γε ‘it, the deer’, and ὠκύς ‘swift’. ὠμοφάγοι is ‘raw-eating’ (ὠμός + φαγ-), and δαρδάπτουσιν ‘tear’. νέμος is a wooded pasture or glen, here in the dative νέμεϊ, with σκιερῷ ‘shady’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 480.

sentences.t:
ἐπί τε λῖν ἤγαγε δαίμων
σίντην·
sentences.tr:
epi te lin ēgage daimōn
sintēn·
sentences.l:
and upon them a power brings a lion,
a ravager;
sentences.i: then some power brings upon them a ravaging lion;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 480. ἐπί … ἤγαγε is tmesis, ‘brought upon’; the aorist again states what always happens. λῖν is the accusative of λίς ‘lion’, and σίντης is ‘ravager’ (σίνομαι ‘harm’). δαίμων is the unnamed divine power that arranges events, here ‘some power’ and not a god by name.

sentences.t: θῶες μέν τε διέτρεσαν, αὐτὰρ ὃ δάπτει·
sentences.tr: thōes men te dietresan, autar ho daptei·
sentences.l: the jackals scatter in fright, but he devours;
sentences.i: the jackals scatter in fright, but he devours it;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 481. διέτρεσαν is the aorist of διατρέω ‘flee in fear, scatter’, used of what always happens; the same verb is used of the Trojans at 486. ὃ is the lion, and δάπτει ‘devours, rends’. In the comparison that follows, the lion is Ajax.

sentences.t:
ὥς ῥα τότ’ ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆα δαΐφρονα ποικιλομήτην
Τρῶες ἕπον πολλοί τε καὶ ἄλκιμοι, αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἥρως
ἀΐσσων ᾧ ἔγχει ἀμύνετο νηλεὲς ἦμαρ.
sentences.tr:
hōs rha tot’ amph’ Odysēa daïphrona poikilomētēn
Trōes hepon polloi te kai alkimoi, autar ho g’ hērōs
aïssōn hōi enchei amyneto nēlees ēmar.
sentences.l:
So then around Odysseus, wise-minded, of many-colored cunning,
the Trojans kept close, many and valiant, but he, the hero,
darting with his own spear, warded off the pitiless day.
sentences.i: So the Trojans, many and valiant, kept close around wise-hearted Odysseus, full of shifting cunning, but the hero, darting with his own spear, warded off the pitiless day.
sentences.n: ὥς ῥα τότ’ ‘so then’ closes the simile. Odysseus’ epithets are δαΐφρονα ‘wise-minded’ (the sense is disputed) and ποικιλομήτην ‘of many-colored cunning’ (ποικίλος ‘many-colored’ + μῆτις); both are stock phrases and translated every time. ἕπον is the same verb as ἕπονθ’ in 474, ‘kept close’. ἄλκιμοι is ‘valiant’. ἥρως ‘hero’ is a title. ἀΐσσων is ‘darting’, ᾧ ἔγχει ‘with his own spear’ (ὅς, ἥ, ὅν as a possessive), and ἀμύνετο the imperfect of ἀμύνομαι ‘ward off from oneself’. νηλεὲς ἦμαρ is ‘the pitiless day’, the day of death.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ ἐγγύθεν ἦλθε φέρων σάκος ἠΰτε πύργον,
στῆ δὲ παρέξ·
sentences.tr:
Aias d’ engythen ēlthe pherōn sakos ēÿte pyrgon,
stē de parex·
sentences.l:
And Ajax from close by came, bearing his shield like a tower,
and stood beside him;
sentences.i: And Ajax came up from close by, carrying a shield like a tower, and stood at his side;
sentences.n: Line 485 is 7.219, where the tower-shield is described at length. ἐγγύθεν ἦλθε is ‘came from close by’ (the suffix -θεν), and ἠΰτε ‘like’. στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘stood’ without augment, and παρέξ ‘out beside, alongside’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 486.

sentences.t: Τρῶες δὲ διέτρεσαν ἄλλυδις ἄλλος.
sentences.tr: Trōes de dietresan allydis allos.
sentences.l: and the Trojans scattered in fright, one this way, one that.
sentences.i: and the Trojans scattered in fright, one this way and one that.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 486. διέτρεσαν ‘scattered in fright’ is the verb used of the jackals at 481, so what the simile pictured now happens: Ajax is the lion. ἄλλυδις ἄλλος is ‘one to one place, another to another’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι τὸν Μενέλαος ἀρήϊος ἔξαγ’ ὁμίλου
χειρὸς ἔχων, εἷος θεράπων σχεδὸν ἤλασεν ἵππους.
sentences.tr:
ētoi ton Menelaos arēïos exag’ homilou
cheiros echōn, heios therapōn schedon ēlasen hippous.
sentences.l:
Indeed him Menelaus, warlike, led out of the throng,
holding him by the hand, until his attendant drove the horses near.
sentences.i: Warlike Menelaus led him out of the throng, holding him by the hand, until his attendant drove the horses up close.
sentences.n: ἤτοι is ‘indeed’, and τὸν the pronoun ‘him’, Odysseus. ἔξαγ’ is the imperfect of ἐξάγω ‘lead out’, with ὁμίλου the genitive of separation, ‘out of the throng’; χειρὸς ἔχων is ‘holding by the hand’ (partitive genitive). εἷος is the epic form of ἕως ‘until’. θεράπων is an ‘attendant’, Menelaus’ own, not named. σχεδόν is ‘near’, and ἤλασεν the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’. ἀρήϊος is ‘warlike’.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δὲ Τρώεσσιν ἐπάλμενος εἷλε Δόρυκλον
Πριαμίδην νόθον υἱόν, ἔπειτα δὲ Πάνδοκον οὖτα,
οὖτα δὲ Λύσανδρον καὶ Πύρασον ἠδὲ Πυλάρτην.
sentences.tr:
Aias de Trōessin epalmenos heile Doryklon
Priamidēn nothon huion, epeita de Pandokon outa,
outa de Lysandron kai Pyrason ēde Pylartēn.
sentences.l:
And Ajax, springing upon the Trojans, took Doryclus,
Priam’s-son, a bastard son, and then Pandocus he wounded,
he wounded Lysander, and Pyrasus, and Pylartes.
sentences.i: Ajax sprang upon the Trojans and killed Doryclus, an illegitimate son of Priam, and then stabbed Pandocus; he stabbed Lysander, and Pyrasus, and Pylartes.
sentences.n: Ajax’ rampage begins with five names. ἐπάλμενος is the aorist participle of ἐπάλλομαι ‘leap upon’ with the dative Τρώεσσιν; εἷλε is ‘took’, here ‘killed’, and οὖτα ‘wounded’ (οὐτάω, the close thrust) without augment. Πριαμίδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Priam’, and νόθος ‘bastard’. The Greek does not say whether the four victims of οὖτα die.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὁπότε πλήθων ποταμὸς πεδίον δὲ κάτεισι
χειμάρρους κατ’ ὄρεσφιν ὀπαζόμενος Διὸς ὄμβρῳ,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hopote plēthōn potamos pedion de kateisi
cheimarrous kat’ oresphin opazomenos Dios ombrōi,
sentences.l:
And as when a river in spate down to the plain goes down,
a winter-flowing one from the mountains, driven on by the rain of Zeus,
sentences.i: As when a river in flood comes down to the plain, a winter torrent from the mountains, driven on by the rain of Zeus,
sentences.n: A second simile, of Ajax as a flooded torrent. ὡς δ’ ὁπότε is ‘and as when’. πλήθων is the participle of πλήθω ‘be full, swell’; κάτεισι is ‘goes down’ (κατά + εἶμι) and πεδίον δέ ‘to the plain’ with the suffix -δε. χειμάρρους is ‘winter-flowing’, a torrent that runs only in the rains. κατ’ ὄρεσφιν is ‘down from the mountains’, and ὀπαζόμενος ‘driven on’ (ὀπάζω ‘make follow’). Διὸς ὄμβρῳ is ‘by the rain of Zeus’: rain is sent by the god.

sentences.t:
πολλὰς δὲ δρῦς ἀζαλέας, πολλὰς δέ τε πεύκας
ἐσφέρεται, πολλὸν δέ τ’ ἀφυσγετὸν εἰς ἅλα βάλλει,
sentences.tr:
pollas de drys azaleas, pollas de te peukas
espheretai, pollon de t’ aphysgeton eis hala ballei,
sentences.l:
and many dry oaks, and many pines
it carries in, and much silt into the sea it casts,
sentences.i: and carries in many dry oaks and many pines, and casts much silt into the sea,
sentences.n: Three πολλ- words in two lines give the weight of the flood. δρῦς and πεύκας are the accusative plurals of ‘oak’ and ‘pine’, ἀζαλέας ‘dry’. ἐσφέρεται is ‘carries in with it’, and ἀφυσγετόν ‘silt, rubbish’, the mud a flood brings down.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφεπε κλονέων πεδίον τότε φαίδιμος Αἴας,
δαΐζων ἵππους τε καὶ ἀνέρας·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephepe kloneōn pedion tote phaidimos Aias,
daïzōn hippous te kai aneras·
sentences.l:
so then pressed on, throwing the plain into confusion, glorious Ajax,
cutting down horses and men;
sentences.i: so glorious Ajax pressed on, throwing the plain into confusion and cutting down horses and men;
sentences.n: ὣς … marks the end of the comparison: ‘so’. ἔφεπε is the imperfect of ἐφέπω ‘pursue, press on’, κλονέων the participle of κλονέω ‘throw into confusion’ with πεδίον ‘the plain’, and δαΐζων ‘cutting down’. φαίδιμος Αἴας is ‘glorious Ajax’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 497.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ πω Ἕκτωρ
πεύθετ’, ἐπεί ῥα μάχης ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ μάρνατο πάσης
ὄχθας πὰρ ποταμοῖο Σκαμάνδρου,
sentences.tr:
oude pō Hektōr
peuthet’, epei rha machēs ep’ aristera marnato pasēs
ochthas par potamoio Skamandrou,
sentences.l:
and not yet did Hector
learn of it, since on the left of all the battle he was fighting
by the banks of the river Scamander,
sentences.i: Hector had not yet learned of it, since he was fighting on the left of the whole battle, by the banks of the river Scamander,
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 497. οὐδέ πω is ‘nor yet’. πεύθετ’ is ‘learned’, the imperfect or aorist of πεύθομαι without augment. ἐπεί ῥα is ‘since’, ἐπ’ ἀριστερά ‘on the left’, and μάρνατο the imperfect of μάρναμαι ‘fight’. ὄχθας πὰρ ποταμοῖο is ‘by the banks of the river’; Σκαμάνδρου is the river Scamander.

sentences.t:
τῇ ῥα μάλιστα
ἀνδρῶν πῖπτε κάρηνα, βοὴ δ’ ἄσβεστος ὀρώρει
Νέστορά τ’ ἀμφὶ μέγαν καὶ ἀρήϊον Ἰδομενῆα.
sentences.tr:
tēi rha malista
andrōn pipte karēna, boē d’ asbestos orōrei
Nestora t’ amphi megan kai arēïon Idomenēa.
sentences.l:
where indeed most
of men fell the heads, and an unquenchable war-cry had arisen
around Nestor, great, and warlike Idomeneus.
sentences.i: where the heads of men fell thickest, and a war-cry that would never go out had arisen around great Nestor and warlike Idomeneus.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 499. τῇ ῥα μάλιστα is ‘where indeed most’. κάρηνα ‘heads’ stand for the men themselves (of mountains, κάρηνα are ‘peaks’), and πῖπτε is an imperfect without augment, ‘kept falling’. ἄσβεστος is ‘unquenchable’ (ἀ- + σβέννυμι, a word of fire); βοή is a ‘war-cry’, and ὀρώρει the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι, ‘had arisen’. ἀμφί stands after its noun in Νέστορά τ’ ἀμφί. ἀρήϊος is ‘warlike’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ μὲν μετὰ τοῖσιν ὁμίλει μέρμερα ῥέζων
ἔγχεΐ θ’ ἱπποσύνῃ τε, νέων δ’ ἀλάπαζε φάλαγγας·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr men meta toisin homilei mermera rhezōn
encheï th’ hipposynēi te, neōn d’ alapaze phalangas·
sentences.l:
Hector, for his part, among them mingled, doing baneful things,
with spear and with horsemanship, and was laying waste the battle-lines of the young men;
sentences.i: Hector, for his part, mingled among them, doing baneful things with spear and horsemanship, and was laying waste the battle-lines of the young men;
sentences.n: The scene shifts to Hector, who is fighting elsewhere (498–499). μετὰ τοῖσιν ‘among them’ does not say whom; ὁμίλει is the imperfect of ὁμιλέω ‘be in the throng, mingle’. μέρμερα ῥέζων ‘doing baneful things’ is a formula (ῥέζω ‘do’). ἱπποσύνῃ is the skill of fighting from a chariot, ‘horsemanship’. ἀλάπαζε is ‘was laying waste’, and νέων the genitive plural of νέος ‘young’, not of ναῦς ‘ship’. φάλαγγας are ‘battle-lines’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄν πω χάζοντο κελεύθου δῖοι Ἀχαιοὶ
εἰ μὴ Ἀλέξανδρος Ἑλένης πόσις ἠϋκόμοιο
παῦσεν ἀριστεύοντα Μαχάονα ποιμένα λαῶν,
ἰῷ τριγλώχινι βαλὼν κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον.
sentences.tr:
oud’ an pō chazonto keleuthou dioi Achaioi
ei mē Alexandros Helenēs posis ēÿkomoio
pausen aristeuonta Machaona poimena laōn,
iōi triglōchini balōn kata dexion ōmon.
sentences.l:
Nor yet would they have been giving ground from the way, the heavenly Achaeans,
had not Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen,
stopped Machaon, shepherd of the people, as he excelled,
having hit him with a three-barbed arrow on the right shoulder.
sentences.i: Nor would the heavenly Achaeans yet have been giving ground, had not Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen, stopped Machaon, shepherd of the people, as he was excelling, by hitting him on the right shoulder with a three-barbed arrow.
sentences.n: A past unreal condition: οὐδ’ ἄν … χάζοντο (ἄν with an imperfect) ‘would not have been giving ground’, and εἰ μή … παῦσεν (aorist) ‘if he had not stopped’. κελεύθου is a genitive of separation, ‘from the way’. Ἑλένης πόσις ἠϋκόμοιο is ‘husband of fine-haired Helen’ (the OCT prints the diaeresis on ἠϋκόμοιο), that is Alexander. ἀριστεύοντα is ‘excelling, being the best’, and ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’. τριγλώχινι (dative, agreeing with ἰῷ) is ‘three-pointed’ or ‘three-barbed’ (γλωχίς ‘barb, point’); the Greek does not settle which. βαλών is ‘having hit’, and κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον ‘on the right shoulder’. Machaon, a healer, is now wounded.

sentences.t:
τῷ ῥα περίδεισαν μένεα πνείοντες Ἀχαιοὶ
μή πώς μιν πολέμοιο μετακλινθέντος ἕλοιεν.
sentences.tr:
tōi rha perideisan menea pneiontes Achaioi
mē pōs min polemoio metaklinthentos heloien.
sentences.l:
For him, then, they were greatly afraid, breathing might, the Achaeans,
lest in some way, the war having turned, they take him.
sentences.i: The Achaeans, breathing might, were greatly afraid for him, in case the Trojans might somehow take him as the battle turned.
sentences.n: τῷ ῥα περίδεισαν is ‘for him, then, they feared greatly’ (περιδείδω with the dative). μένεα πνείοντες ‘breathing might’ is a formula. μή with the optative ἕλοιεν is ‘lest they take him’; the subject, the Trojans, is not stated. μετακλινθέντος is an aorist passive participle of μετακλίνω ‘turn about’, in a genitive absolute with πολέμοιο ‘the war’.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ Ἰδομενεὺς προσεφώνεε Νέστορα δῖον·
sentences.tr: autika d’ Idomeneus prosephōnee Nestora dion·
sentences.l: And at once Idomeneus addressed Nestor, heavenly:
sentences.i: At once Idomeneus spoke to heavenly Nestor:
sentences.n: αὐτίκα is ‘at once’, and προσεφώνεε the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘address’. δῖον ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet; here it is Nestor’s, and it is translated the same way as for Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ὦ Νέστορ Νηληϊάδη μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν
ἄγρει σῶν ὀχέων ἐπιβήσεο, πὰρ δὲ Μαχάων
βαινέτω, ἐς νῆας δὲ τάχιστ’ ἔχε μώνυχας ἵππους·
sentences.tr:
ō Nestor Nēlēïadē mega kydos Achaiōn
agrei sōn ocheōn epibēseo, par de Machaōn
bainetō, es nēas de tachist’ eche mōnychas hippous·
sentences.i: “Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans, come, mount your chariot, and let Machaon go up beside you, and drive the solid-hoofed horses to the ships as fast as you can;
sentences.n: Idomeneus speaks, and the first line is 10.87 word for word (it is the same address to Nestor). Νηληϊάδη is a patronymic, ‘son of Neleus’. ἄγρει is the exclamation ‘come’. ἐπιβήσεο is an aorist imperative, ‘mount’, with the genitive σῶν ὀχέων ‘your chariot’ (ὄχεα, plural for one chariot). πὰρ δέ is ‘and beside’, βαινέτω the third-person imperative ‘let him go’. ἔχε is ‘keep, drive’, with ἐς νῆας ‘to the ships’ and τάχιστα ‘as quickly as possible’. μώνυχας ἵππους are ‘solid-hoofed horses’ (μώνυξ ‘with an undivided hoof’).

sentences.t:
ἰητρὸς γὰρ ἀνὴρ πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων
ἰούς τ’ ἐκτάμνειν ἐπί τ’ ἤπια φάρμακα πάσσειν.
sentences.tr:
iētros gar anēr pollōn antaxios allōn
ious t’ ektamnein epi t’ ēpia pharmaka passein.
sentences.l:
for a healer, a man, of equal worth to many others,
to cut out arrows and to sprinkle on gentle drugs.”
sentences.i: for a healer is worth as much as many other men, for cutting out arrows and sprinkling on gentle drugs.”
sentences.n: The reason for saving Machaon. ἰητρός is ‘healer’, and ἀντάξιος takes the genitive πολλῶν ἄλλων ‘equal in worth to many others’. ἐκτάμνειν ‘to cut out’ and πάσσειν ‘to sprinkle’ are infinitives that say what he is worth in; ἐπί … πάσσειν is tmesis. ἰούς are ‘arrows’, and ἤπια φάρμακα ‘gentle drugs’. The speech ends.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, oud’ apithēse Gerēnios hippota Nestōr.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and did not disobey, the Gerenian horseman Nestor.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the Gerenian horseman Nestor did not disobey him.
sentences.n: A formula line, word for word the same as 8.112. ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he spoke’; ἀπίθησε is the aorist of ἀπιθέω ‘disobey’. Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ is the Gerenian horseman Nestor: the meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed (Gerenia in Messenia, or from γέρων ‘old man’ or γέρας ‘honour’).

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ ὧν ὀχέων ἐπεβήσετο, πὰρ δὲ Μαχάων
βαῖν’ Ἀσκληπιοῦ υἱὸς ἀμύμονος ἰητῆρος·
sentences.tr:
autika d’ hōn ocheōn epebēseto, par de Machaōn
bain’ Asklēpiou huios amymonos iētēros·
sentences.l:
And at once he mounted his own chariot, and beside him Machaon
went, the son of Asclepius, the blameless healer;
sentences.i: At once he mounted his own chariot, and Machaon, son of Asclepius the blameless healer, went up beside him;
sentences.n: ὧν is the possessive ‘own’ (genitive plural of ὅς, agreeing with ὀχέων), not Ionic οὖν: ‘his own chariot’, answering σῶν ὀχέων ‘your chariot’ in 512. ἐπεβήσετο is the aorist of ἐπιβαίνομαι ‘mount’, with the genitive ὀχέων. βαῖν’ is an imperfect of βαίνω without augment, with πὰρ ‘beside’. Ἀσκληπιοῦ υἱὸς ἀμύμονος ἰητῆρος is ‘son of Asclepius, the blameless healer’; the sense of ἀμύμων is not known, and ‘blameless’ is the traditional guess.

sentences.t:
μάστιξεν δ’ ἵππους, τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκοντε πετέσθην
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς·
sentences.tr:
mastixen d’ hippous, tō d’ ouk aekonte petesthēn
nēas epi glaphyras·
sentences.l:
and he whipped the horses, and the two, not unwilling, flew
to the hollow ships;
sentences.i: and he whipped the horses, and the pair flew, not unwilling, to the hollow ships;
sentences.n: Line 519 and the first half of 520 are 10.530–531 (the return of Diomedes and Odysseus). μάστιξεν is the aorist of μαστίζω ‘whip’. τὼ is the dual pronoun ‘those two’, the two horses, with the dual ἀέκοντε ‘unwilling’ and the dual verb πετέσθην ‘flew’. νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς is ‘to the hollow ships’ with ἐπί after its noun. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 520.

sentences.t: τῇ γὰρ φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ.
sentences.tr: tēi gar philon epleto thymōi.
sentences.l: for thither it was dear to their spirit.
sentences.i: for it pleased their spirit to go that way.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 520. τῇ is ‘thither’, φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ ‘was dear to the spirit’ (ἔπλετο is the aorist or imperfect of πέλομαι ‘be, become’), and the Greek does not say whose spirit: ‘their’ is supplied, the horses just called ‘not unwilling’, though Nestor and Machaon cannot be ruled out. Line 520 is 10.531 word for word.

sentences.t:
Κεβριόνης δὲ Τρῶας ὀρινομένους ἐνόησεν
Ἕκτορι παρβεβαώς, καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr:
Kebrionēs de Trōas orinomenous enoēsen
Hektori parbebaōs, kai min pros mython eeipen·
sentences.l:
And Cebriones the Trojans, being thrown into turmoil, noticed,
standing beside Hector, and addressed him with a word:
sentences.i: And Cebriones, standing beside Hector, noticed the Trojans being thrown into turmoil, and spoke to him:
sentences.n: ὀρινομένους is the passive participle of ὀρίνω ‘stir up, throw into turmoil’, and ἐνόησεν the aorist of νοέω ‘notice’. Ἕκτορι παρβεβαώς is the perfect participle of παραβαίνω ‘stand beside’ (the form παρβεβαώς is shortened), with the dative. καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν ‘and addressed him with a word’ is the formula heard at 440.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ νῶϊ μὲν ἐνθάδ’ ὁμιλέομεν Δαναοῖσιν
ἐσχατιῇ πολέμοιο δυσηχέος·
sentences.tr:
Hektor nōï men enthad’ homileomen Danaoisin
eschatiēi polemoio dysēcheos·
sentences.l:
“Hector, we two here are mingling with the Danaans
at the edge of ill-sounding war;
sentences.i: “Hector, we two are here mingling with the Danaans at the edge of the ill-sounding war;
sentences.n: Cebriones speaks to Hector. νῶϊ is the dual pronoun ‘we two’, with the plural verb ὁμιλέομεν ‘we mingle, are in the throng with’ and the dative Δαναοῖσιν. ἐσχατιῇ is ‘at the edge’, and πολέμοιο δυσηχέος ‘of ill-sounding war’ (δυσ- ‘ill’ + ἦχος ‘sound’). The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 524.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι
Τρῶες ὀρίνονται ἐπιμὶξ ἵπποι τε καὶ αὐτοί.
sentences.tr:
hoi de dē alloi
Trōes orinontai epimix hippoi te kai autoi.
sentences.l:
but those others
Trojans are thrown into turmoil, in confusion, both horses and themselves.
sentences.i: but the rest of the Trojans are thrown into turmoil, in confusion, the horses and the men themselves.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 524. οἳ δὲ δὴ ἄλλοι Τρῶες is ‘but those others, the Trojans’. ὀρίνονται is the passive of ὀρίνω, the verb of 521. ἐπιμίξ ‘in confusion’ is a rare adverb from the root of μίγνυμι ‘mix’. ἵπποι τε καὶ αὐτοί is ‘both horses and themselves’, the men.

sentences.t: Αἴας δὲ κλονέει Τελαμώνιος· εὖ δέ μιν ἔγνων·
sentences.tr: Aias de kloneei Telamōnios· eu de min egnōn·
sentences.l: And Ajax is throwing into confusion, the Telamonian; and well I recognised him;
sentences.i: Telamonian Ajax is throwing them into confusion, and I recognised him well;
sentences.n: κλονέει is the present of κλονέω ‘throw into confusion’, with the Trojans understood as its object. Τελαμώνιος ‘Telamonian’ tells this Ajax from the other. ἔγνων is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise’, and εὖ ‘well’; the next line gives Cebriones’ reason.

sentences.t: εὐρὺ γὰρ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ἔχει σάκος·
sentences.tr: eury gar amph’ ōmoisin echei sakos·
sentences.l: for broad about his shoulders he has the shield;
sentences.i: for he carries a broad shield about his shoulders;
sentences.n: εὐρύ is ‘broad’, agreeing with σάκος ‘shield’, which hangs ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ‘about the shoulders’ (dative plural in -οισιν). It is the great shield of 485, and the reason Cebriones knows him. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 527.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡμεῖς
κεῖσ’ ἵππους τε καὶ ἅρμ’ ἰθύνομεν, ἔνθα μάλιστα
ἱππῆες πεζοί τε κακὴν ἔριδα προβαλόντες
ἀλλήλους ὀλέκουσι, βοὴ δ’ ἄσβεστος ὄρωρεν.
sentences.tr:
alla kai hēmeis
keis’ hippous te kai harm’ ithynomen, entha malista
hippēes pezoi te kakēn erida probalontes
allēlous olekousi, boē d’ asbestos orōren.
sentences.l:
but we too
thither horses and chariot let us steer, where most
horsemen and men on foot, having cast forward evil strife,
are destroying one another, and an unquenchable war-cry has arisen.”
sentences.i: but let us too steer our horses and chariot to the place where, most of all, mounted men and men on foot, having cast forward evil strife, are destroying one another, and a war-cry that will not go out has arisen.”
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 527. ἰθύνομεν is the short-vowel subjunctive of ἰθύνω ‘steer’ (‘let us steer’), and κεῖσ’ is ἐκεῖσε ‘thither’. ἔνθα μάλιστα is ‘where most’. ἱππῆες is ‘horsemen’ and πεζοί ‘men on foot’. προβαλόντες ‘having cast forward’ is from προβάλλω ‘throw forward’, and the exact picture of ‘casting forward strife’ is not clear. ὀλέκουσι is ‘destroy’. ὄρωρεν is the perfect of ὄρνυμι, ‘has arisen’, as ὀρώρει at 500. The speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἵμασεν καλλίτριχας ἵππους
μάστιγι λιγυρῇ·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas himasen kallitrichas hippous
mastigi ligyrēi·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, he lashed the fair-maned horses
with a clear-sounding whip;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and lashed the fair-maned horses with a clear-sounding whip;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is ‘so then speaking’, and the subject is Cebriones. ἵμασεν is the aorist of ἱμάσσω ‘lash’. καλλίτριχας ἵππους ‘fair-maned horses’ is a formula (see 8.503 and the Odyssey). μάστιγι λιγυρῇ is the dative of means, ‘with a clear-sounding whip’ (λιγυρός ‘clear-sounding’). The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 532.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ πληγῆς ἀΐοντες
ῥίμφ’ ἔφερον θοὸν ἅρμα μετὰ Τρῶας καὶ Ἀχαιοὺς
στείβοντες νέκυάς τε καὶ ἀσπίδας·
sentences.tr:
toi de plēgēs aïontes
rhimph’ epheron thoon harma meta Trōas kai Achaious
steibontes nekyas te kai aspidas·
sentences.i: and the horses, hearing the lash, carried the swift chariot lightly among the Trojans and Achaeans, treading on the dead and on shields;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 532. τοί is the pronoun ‘they’, the horses, and πληγῆς the genitive of the stroke they hear (ἀΐοντες, from ἀΐω ‘hear’). ῥίμφα is ‘lightly’, θοόν ‘swift’, and ἔφερον ‘bore’. νέκυας is the accusative plural of νέκυς, ‘the dead’, the lifeless body; στείβοντες is ‘treading on’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 534.

sentences.t:
αἵματι δ’ ἄξων
νέρθεν ἅπας πεπάλακτο καὶ ἄντυγες αἳ περὶ δίφρον,
ἃς ἄρ’ ἀφ’ ἱππείων ὁπλέων ῥαθάμιγγες ἔβαλλον
αἵ τ’ ἀπ’ ἐπισσώτρων.
sentences.tr:
haimati d’ axōn
nerthen hapas pepalakto kai antyges hai peri diphron,
has ar’ aph’ hippeiōn hopleōn rhathaminges eballon
hai t’ ap’ epissōtrōn.
sentences.l:
and with blood the axle
underneath was all spattered, and the rails that run around the chariot,
which the drops from the horses’ hooves struck
and those from the tires.
sentences.i: and the axle underneath was all spattered with blood, and the rails around the chariot, which drops from the horses’ hooves struck, and those from the tires.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 534. πεπάλακτο is the pluperfect passive of παλάσσω ‘spatter, stain’, with αἵματι ‘with blood’; νέρθεν ‘from below’ and ἅπας ‘all’. ἄντυγες are the ‘rails’ of the chariot-box (as at 5.728), and δίφρον here is the chariot (the same word is a stool at 3.424). ἱππείων ὁπλέων is ‘of horses’ hooves’, ῥαθάμιγγες ‘drops’, and ἐπίσσωτρα the metal ‘tires’ round the wheels. The unit ends at the full stop in the middle of 537.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ ἵετο δῦναι ὅμιλον
ἀνδρόμεον ῥῆξαί τε μετάλμενος· ἐν δὲ κυδοιμὸν
ἧκε κακὸν Δαναοῖσι, μίνυνθα δὲ χάζετο δουρός.
sentences.tr:
ho de hieto dynai homilon
andromeon rhēxai te metalmenos· en de kydoimon
hēke kakon Danaoisi, minyntha de chazeto douros.
sentences.l:
And he was eager to plunge into the throng
human, and to break it, leaping in; and into it uproar
evil he sent for the Danaans, and for a little while he gave ground from the spear.
sentences.i: And he was eager to plunge into the throng of men and break it, leaping in among them; and he sent evil uproar among the Danaans, and gave ground from the spear for only a little while.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of 537. ὃ δέ is Hector; ἵετο is the imperfect of ἵεμαι ‘be eager’, with the infinitives δῦναι ‘to plunge into’ (with the accusative ὅμιλον) and ῥῆξαι ‘to break’. ἀνδρόμεον is ‘of men, human’ (as in ἀνδρόμεα κρέα, ‘human flesh’), and μετάλμενος the aorist participle of μεθάλλομαι ‘leap in among’. ἐν … ἧκε is tmesis, ‘sent in’. κυδοιμός is ‘uproar’. μίνυνθα δὲ χάζετο δουρός is ‘and for a little while he gave ground from the spear’; the Greek does not say whose spear, but the sense is that he held back only briefly.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ τῶν ἄλλων ἐπεπωλεῖτο στίχας ἀνδρῶν
ἔγχεΐ τ’ ἄορί τε μεγάλοισί τε χερμαδίοισιν,
Αἴαντος δ’ ἀλέεινε μάχην Τελαμωνιάδαο.
sentences.tr:
autar ho tōn allōn epepōleito stichas andrōn
encheï t’ aori te megaloisi te chermadioisin,
Aiantos d’ aleeine machēn Telamōniadao.
sentences.l:
But he, of the other men, was going about the ranks,
with spear and with sword and with great stones,
and Ajax’s fighting he avoided, Telamon’s son’s.
sentences.i: But he ranged along the ranks of the other men with spear and sword and great stones, while he shunned the fighting of Ajax, son of Telamon.
sentences.n: Hector goes through the other ranks and avoids Ajax. Lines 540–541 are 11.264–265 word for word (there of Agamemnon): ἐπεπωλεῖτο is ‘ranged along’, and χερμάδια are stones that fill the hand. ἀλέεινε is the form of ἀλεείνω ‘avoid, shun’, and Τελαμωνιάδαο the patronymic ‘son of Telamon’ in the genitive in -αο. The edition has no line 543: its numbering jumps from 542 to 544, and the next part begins at 544.
